tasks.description: Import the math module. Print the square root of 144.
tasks.hint:
`import math` at the top gives you access to all math functions.
Access them with dot notation: `math.sqrt(144)`
`math.sqrt()` always returns a float, so the result is `12.0`.
tasks.walkthrough:
`import math` loads the module. `math.sqrt` is the square root function inside it.
It always returns a float, so 12 appears as 12.0.

tasks.description: Import only pi from the math module. Print it rounded to 5 decimal places.
tasks.hint:
`from math import pi` imports just `pi` — you can use it directly without `math.pi`.
`round(pi, 5)` rounds to 5 decimal places.
Result: `3.14159`
tasks.walkthrough:
This style imports only `pi`, so it's used on its own without `math.` in front.
`round(pi, 5)` trims it to five decimal places.

tasks.description: Use math.ceil() and math.floor() on 3.7. Print both results on separate lines.
tasks.hint:
`math.ceil(3.7)` rounds UP to the nearest integer → `4`
`math.floor(3.7)` rounds DOWN to the nearest integer → `3`
These always return integers, unlike `round()` which rounds to nearest.
tasks.walkthrough:
`ceil` always rounds up to the next whole number, `floor` always rounds down.
Unlike `round()`, they ignore how close the number is to either side.

tasks.description: Import random. Use random.randint() to print 3 random numbers between 1 and 6 (like dice rolls).
tasks.hint:
`random.randint(a, b)` returns a random integer where `a <= result <= b` (BOTH ends inclusive).
`random.randint(1, 6)` simulates a dice roll.
The numbers will be different each run — that's expected behaviour.
tasks.walkthrough:
The loop runs three times and each pass asks for a fresh random number from 1 to 6 inclusive.
Your numbers will differ from anyone else's, which is why this task isn't checked automatically.

tasks.description: Use random.choice() to pick a random item from ['rock', 'paper', 'scissors'] and print it.
tasks.hint:
`random.choice(sequence)` picks one random element from any sequence.
Pass your list directly: `random.choice(['rock', 'paper', 'scissors'])`
The result changes each run.
tasks.walkthrough: `random.choice()` takes any list and returns one of its items at random.

tasks.description: Use random.shuffle() to shuffle the list [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and print the shuffled list.
tasks.hint:
`random.shuffle(list)` modifies the list IN PLACE — it doesn't return a new list.
Call it, then print the list: `random.shuffle(nums); print(nums)`
Don't do `print(random.shuffle(nums))` — that prints `None`!
tasks.walkthrough:
`shuffle` rearranges the list you give it and returns nothing.
That's why the shuffle and the print are two separate lines.

tasks.description: Use the math module to find the value of 2 to the power of 10 using math.pow(). Print as an integer.
tasks.hint:
`math.pow(base, exp)` returns a float: `math.pow(2, 10)` → `1024.0`
Wrap in `int()` to convert to an integer: `print(int(math.pow(2, 10)))` → `1024`
Alternative: `2 ** 10` uses Python's built-in exponent operator.
tasks.walkthrough:
`math.pow(2, 10)` gives the float 1024.0.
Wrapping it in `int()` drops the decimal part so the printed result is 1024.

lesson.intro:
Python ships with a big library of ready-made code, split into modules. Square
roots, random numbers, dates, file handling: someone has already written it.
`import` is how you bring a module into your program.

sections.heading: import module, then module.thing
sections.body:
After `import math`, everything in the math module is reachable with a dot.
The dot says "look inside math for this". Imports normally go at the top of
the file.
sections.code:
import math

print(math.sqrt(144))
print(math.pi)
print(math.ceil(3.2), math.floor(3.8))

sections.heading: from module import name
sections.body:
If you only need one or two things, you can import them directly and use them
without the module prefix. Both styles are fine; the first is clearer about
where things come from, the second is shorter.
sections.code:
from math import pi, sqrt

print(round(pi, 5))
print(sqrt(81))

sections.heading: The random module
sections.body:
`randint(a, b)` gives a whole number between a and b, both included.
`choice()` picks an item from a list. `shuffle()` mixes a list up in place.
The output changes every run, which is the point.
sections.code:
import random

print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.choice(['rock', 'paper', 'scissors']))
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
random.shuffle(nums)
print(nums)

sections.heading: Floats from math functions
sections.body:
Most math functions return floats, even for whole answers: `math.pow(2, 10)`
is `1024.0`. Wrap in `int()` if you want the integer, or use Python's own `**`
operator, which keeps integers as integers.

watch_out: Using `sqrt(144)` after `import math` without the `math.` prefix gives a NameError. Either write `math.sqrt` or use `from math import sqrt`.
Naming your own file `random.py` or `math.py`. Python will import your file instead of the real module.
`random.shuffle(nums)` returns `None`. Shuffle first, then print the list on the next line.
`randint(1, 6)` includes 6. `range(1, 6)` doesn't. They disagree on purpose, annoyingly.
